solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Spot right idiot in wrinkly fabric

parts.note: to spot something is to see it
a sucker is a gullible fool

explanation.surface: A tailor notices a fool dressed in crumpled cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: Seersucker is a thin cotton cloth woven with a puckered, crinkled surface.

clue.text: One who's quick to obtain drink, holding head

indicators.note: holding means the drink word wraps around the head word

parts.note: to sup is to drink
napper is British slang for the head

explanation.surface: Someone grabs a drink while clutching their head.
explanation.walkthrough: Snapper-up comes from Shakespeare's 'snapper-up of unconsidered trifles'.
explanation.definitionFit: A snapper-up is someone who seizes things eagerly, grabbing them before others can.

clue.text: First person set up police force, getting local six-footer

indicators.note: set up in a down clue means raised, so the pronoun is read bottom to top

parts.note: me is the first person pronoun
the Met is London's Metropolitan Police

explanation.surface: I establish a police force and recruit a local insect.
explanation.walkthrough: Emmet is a dialect word for an ant, which has six legs, hence 'six-footer'; 'local' marks the regional word.
explanation.definitionFit: An emmet is a regional English word for an ant, an insect with six legs.

clue.text: Doctor loudly rebuked how supermarket food may be

parts.note: a shrink is slang for a psychiatrist, a doctor

indicators.note: loudly means spoken aloud, so the word for rebuked is heard as a homophone

parts.note: rapped means reprimanded

explanation.surface: A doctor noisily tells off a supermarket about its food.
explanation.definitionFit: Supermarket goods often come sealed in tight plastic film shrunk onto them by heat.

clue.text: Horse with hardened skin on part of ear

indicators.note: on in a down clue puts the skin word above the horse word

parts.note: a corn is a patch of hardened skin on the foot
a cob is a sturdy short-legged horse

explanation.surface: A horse has callused skin on a part of its ear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ear' is not the hearing organ but an ear of maize.
explanation.definitionFit: The cob is the central woody core of a maize ear on which the kernels grow.

clue.text: Bill could be one in river astride swans

indicators.note: astride means straddling, so the river letters sit either side of the swans

parts.note: the Exe is a river in Devon
a pen is a female swan

explanation.surface: A bird with a bill might be seen on a river with swans either side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' suggests a beak among the swans; it is a bill to pay.
explanation.definitionFit: A bill is a charge to be paid, an example of a cost or outlay.

clue.text: Old people's home had no room, finally

definitions.text: Old people's home had no room, finally

indicators.note: finally asks for the closing letter of each of the four words before it

parts.note: last letter of home
last letter of had
last letter of no
last letter of room

explanation.surface: A care home for the elderly turned people away because it was full.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: the end letters of 'home had no room' spell the answer, and the clue as a whole describes an ancient land, home of the Edomites.
explanation.definitionFit: Edom was the biblical kingdom south of the Dead Sea, homeland of the ancient Edomite nation.

clue.text: Goods to transport? Pack vehicle and then drive

parts.note: a deck is a pack of cards
a car is a vehicle
go means drive, vigour or energy

explanation.surface: Load goods for shipping into a vehicle and set off.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'transport' is a troopship or ship, carrying goods on its deck.
explanation.definitionFit: Deck cargo is freight carried on a ship's open deck rather than in its hold.

clue.text: '60s youths adopting upper-class manner

indicators.note: adopting means taking in, so the class letter goes inside the youths

parts.note: the Mods were a 1960s British youth subculture
U is a label for upper-class usage

explanation.surface: Sixties youngsters take on a posh style.
explanation.definitionFit: Modus is Latin for a way or method, as in modus operandi.

clue.text: One with a suit: a male with more awful clothing

indicators.note: clothing here means wrapping round, so the letters for more awful surround the male

parts.note: direr is the comparative of dire, awful

explanation.surface: A man in a suit is wearing even worse clothes than the others.
explanation.definitionFit: A suitor paying court to someone is their admirer; the suit is a courtship, not a garment.

clue.text: Overly serious, following whizz in school

indicators.note: in signals that following and whizz go inside the school word

parts.note: a pod is a school of whales or dolphins
F is the abbreviation for following, as in page references
an ace is an expert, a whizz

explanation.surface: A pupil seems humourless after being made a star at school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'School' looks like a classroom, but it is a group of whales. Po-faced is British for stiffly solemn or disapproving.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone po-faced wears a humourless, solemn, prim expression, taking things too seriously.

clue.text: Where records go in affair involving current ministers

indicators.note: involving means taking in, so the current letter sits inside the affair

parts.note: a fling is a short affair
I is the symbol for electric current
the Cabinet is the body of senior government ministers

explanation.surface: Records of an affair implicating government ministers are filed away.
explanation.definitionFit: A filing cabinet is office furniture with drawers for storing documents and paperwork.

clue.text: Don still sleeping around

indicators.note: around means turned about, so the phrase for still sleeping is read from the end

parts.note: someone still sleeping is not up yet

explanation.surface: A university fellow is still asleep in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Don' looks like an Oxbridge academic, but it is the verb meaning to dress in.
explanation.definitionFit: To don clothes is to put them on, so the phrasal verb is a straight synonym of the verb.

clue.text: Clashes with crook getting 100 in darts

parts.note: a con is a convict, a crook

indicators.note: in places the hundred inside the word for darts

parts.note: to dart is to flit, moving quickly
C is the Roman numeral for 100

explanation.surface: A criminal scores a ton at the dartboard, sparking arguments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Darts' reads as the pub game, but it is the verb: flits.
explanation.definitionFit: Conflicts are disputes or fights, the same thing as clashes between opposing sides.

clue.text: Wind, say, from a green beer, newly brewed

indicators.note: brewed suggests something mixed up and fermented, so these letters are stirred into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An eco-friendly lager just made at the brewery gives wind.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface hints at the digestive effect of beer; 'wind' is instead wind power.
explanation.definitionFit: Wind is an example of a power source that is replenished naturally, hence 'say' to mark an instance.

clue.text: Distressed annalist penning nothing in papers

indicators.note: penning means enclosing, so the zero letter goes inside the jumbled word
distressed means shaken up, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: O is zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A troubled chronicler writes nothing in the newspapers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Papers' here is the plural noun for newspapers, so the definition matches the plural answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The nationals are newspapers distributed across the whole country, as opposed to local papers.

clue.text: Rabbit gently, at intervals, parting pair of bovines

indicators.note: parting means separating, so the letters split the two yaks

parts.note: two yaks, a yak being a Himalayan ox

indicators.note: at intervals takes every other letter of gently

explanation.surface: A rabbit softly hops between two grazing oxen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rabbit' is not the animal but British slang for chatter, from rhyming slang rabbit and pork, talk.
explanation.definitionFit: Yakety-yak is incessant chatter; in Britain to rabbit on is to talk at length.

clue.text: How one may get remit, perhaps, to regress

parts.note: a clock is a timer, and putting that word back, reading it from the end, gives this word

explanation.surface: A puzzle about how one might obtain an official remit, somehow going backwards.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as an instruction: 'put back' means reverse, and 'the clock' is a TIMER; written backwards that becomes REMIT.
explanation.definitionFit: To put back the clock is an idiom for returning to an earlier, less advanced state of affairs.

clue.text: Maybe one proposing name aboard boat? I don't know

indicators.note: aboard puts the name letter inside the boat

parts.note: a keel is a kind of flat-bottomed boat
er is the hesitation sound of someone unsure

explanation.surface: A sailor proposes naming the boat but is unsure.
explanation.walkthrough: A man proposing marriage traditionally goes down on one knee.
explanation.definitionFit: One proposing marriage traditionally kneels, so such a person is an example of someone kneeling.

clue.text: Remark praising short stockings on Tolstoy heroine

indicators.note: short means the word is cut, losing its last letter

parts.note: hose are stockings
Anna Karenina is Tolstoy's heroine

explanation.surface: Someone compliments a character's short stockings in a Tolstoy novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Hosanna is a cry of adoration and praise to God, used in Christian worship.

clue.text: Lie heavily on stone, at first? This is breaking now

indicators.note: at first puts the stone abbreviation at the front of the word

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for stone, the British unit of weight
to oppress is to weigh heavily on someone

explanation.surface: Someone lies on a heavy rock, then a news flash interrupts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breaking' is the breaking-news sense: news that arrived just as the paper was printing.
explanation.definitionFit: Stop press is late news inserted into a newspaper after printing has begun, just as breaking news arrives.

clue.text: Partners hugging country girl who's sometimes lazy

indicators.note: hugging means enclosing, so the partners wrap round the country

parts.note: South and North are partners at the bridge table
the USA is a country

explanation.surface: Two partners hug a country girl who can be idle.
explanation.walkthrough: A lazy Susan is a revolving tray on a dining table.
explanation.definitionFit: A lazy Susan is a rotating serving tray, so this female name is sometimes paired with lazy.

clue.text: European footballer's caught plague

indicators.note: caught means holding, so the European letter sits inside the footballer

parts.note: George Best was a famous Northern Ireland footballer; the 's means he has caught

explanation.surface: A footballer from Europe has caught a disease.
explanation.walkthrough: George Best was a celebrated Manchester United and Northern Ireland winger of the 1960s.
explanation.definitionFit: To beset is to trouble or harass persistently, just as to plague someone is.

clue.text: Deal with English, entering fight without heart

indicators.note: entering puts the English letter inside the reduced fight word
without heart means losing the central letter of the word

parts.note: a set-to is a fight or argument

explanation.surface: An Englishman joins a half-hearted brawl to settle things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without heart' takes the middle T from SETTO to leave SETO, and E goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: To see to a task is to attend to it or handle it, exactly as dealing with it.

clue.text: Stink about to permeate shoe

indicators.note: to permeate is to spread through, so the about letter goes inside the shoe

parts.note: a sandal is a kind of shoe
C is circa, Latin for about

explanation.surface: A bad smell is spreading through a shoe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stink' looks like a smell, but here it is the uproar sense, as in kicking up a stink.
explanation.definitionFit: A stink is a public fuss or outcry, which is what a scandal causes.

clue.text: New leader leaves artillery where order is put up

indicators.note: the leading letter of the artillery word departs and the new letter replaces it

parts.note: gunnery is the operation of heavy guns, artillery

explanation.surface: A fresh commander quits the artillery, where discipline is imposed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Order' sounds military, but it is a religious order, and 'put up' means housed.
explanation.definitionFit: A convent houses a community of nuns, members of a religious order, so the order lodges there.

clue.text: I won't keep mum's provisions

definitions.note: nosh is a mass noun for food, matching the plural provisions

parts.note: no is a refusal, saying I won't
sh is the command to be quiet, keep mum

explanation.surface: Someone refuses to look after their mother's supplies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mum' is not mother but silent, in 'keep mum'. Nosh is British slang for food.
explanation.definitionFit: Nosh is informal British slang for food, the edible supplies meant by provisions.

clue.text: Defence playing worst during time off

indicators.note: during places the jumbled letters within the time off word

parts.note: a break is time off work

indicators.note: playing suggests the letters are messed about, rearranged

explanation.surface: A team plays its worst defensive game during a holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Defence' sounds like a football back line, but it is a military earthwork.
explanation.definitionFit: A breastwork is a temporary chest-high fortification, a military defence.
